a: son of Gabael, son of Raphael, son of Raguel
p: Sinaiticus adds Raphael and Raguel to Tobit's family tree.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: τοῦ Γαβαὴλ τοῦ Ῥαφαὴλ τοῦ Ῥαγουήλ
readings.en: of Gabael, of Raphael, of Raguel
readings.plain: son of Gabael, son of Raphael, son of Raguel

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: τοῦ Γαβαήλ
readings.plain: son of Gabael

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus, the base text. The two extra names are the names of the angel and of Sarah's father, which may be why a scribe added them, or why the shorter text dropped them.

a: , toward the west, with Phogor to its south
p: Only Sinaiticus adds "toward the west" and "to the left of Phogor".

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ὀπίσω δυσμῶν ἡλίου, ἐξ ἀριστερῶν Φογώρ
readings.en: behind the setting of the sun, on the left of Phogor
readings.plain: , toward the west, with Phogor to its south

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: (lacks the words)

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. Vaticanus also lacks "upper" before Galilee.

a: the house of my ancestor David and from Jerusalem
p: Sinaiticus says Naphtali broke from David's house and Jerusalem; Vaticanus says from "the house of Jerusalem".

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἀπὸ τοῦ οἴκου Δαυεὶδ τοῦ πατρός μου καὶ ἀπὸ Ἰερουσαλήμ
readings.en: from the house of David my father and from Jerusalem
readings.plain: the house of my ancestor David and from Jerusalem

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: ἀπὸ τοῦ οἴκου Ἰεροσολύμων
readings.plain: the house of Jerusalem

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. Its wording recalls 1 Kings 12:16–19, where the north breaks from "the house of David."

a: All my kinsmen and the house of my ancestor Naphtali offered sacrifices on all the mountains of Galilee to the calf that Jeroboam king of Israel had made in Dan
p: Sinaiticus names Jeroboam's calf at Dan; Vaticanus says the rebel tribes sacrificed to "Baal the heifer".

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: πάντες οἱ ἀδελφοί μου καὶ ὁ οἶκος Νεφθαλεὶμ τοῦ πατρός μου, ἐθυσίαζον ἐκεῖνοι τῷ μόσχῳ ὃν ἐποίησεν Ἰεροβεὰμ ὁ βασιλεὺς Ἰσραὴλ ἐν Δὰν ἐπὶ πάντων ὀρέων τῆς Γαλειλαίας
readings.en: all my brothers and the house of Naphtali my father sacrificed to the calf that Jeroboam king of Israel made in Dan, on all the mountains of Galilee
readings.plain: All my kinsmen and the house of my ancestor Naphtali offered sacrifices on all the mountains of Galilee to the calf that Jeroboam king of Israel had made in Dan

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text; also written in the margin of Sinaiticus by a later corrector (ℵc.a)
readings.orig: πᾶσαι αἱ φυλαὶ αἱ συναποστᾶσαι ἔθυον τῇ Βάαλ τῇ δαμάλει, καὶ ὁ οἶκος Νεφθαλεὶμ τοῦ πατρός μου
readings.en: all the tribes that broke away together sacrificed to Baal the heifer, and the house of Naphtali my father
readings.plain: All the tribes that broke away together sacrificed to Baal the heifer, and so did the house of my ancestor Naphtali

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. Vaticanus's "Baal" with the feminine article (tē Baal) is the Septuagint's habit of reading "shame" (Greek aischynē, feminine) in place of Baal, as in Romans 11:4; "the heifer" is a mocking name for the calf (compare Hosea 10:5).
b: Swete's notes report that a later corrector of Sinaiticus (ℵc.a, about the 600s) struck out "all my kinsmen" and wrote the Vaticanus wording in the margin, so replacing Sinaiticus's opening with the shorter text's.

a: Deborah, the mother of our forefather Ananiel
p: Sinaiticus: mother of Ananiel, Tobit's grandfather. Vaticanus: Tobit's father's mother.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: Δεββώρα ἡ μήτηρ Ἁνανιὴλ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν
readings.en: Deborah the mother of Ananiel our father
readings.plain: Deborah, the mother of our forefather Ananiel

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: Δεββώρα ἡ μήτηρ τοῦ πατρός μου
readings.en: Deborah the mother of my father
readings.plain: Deborah, my father's mother

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus, though its "our father" must mean "forefather" to fit 1:1. Vaticanus's whole verse is much shorter: "the third I gave to those to whom it was due."

a: a woman from the descendants of our own family line
p: Vaticanus names Anna at her wedding; Sinaiticus first names her in 1:20.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἔλαβον γυναῖκα ἐκ τοῦ σπέρματος τῆς πατριᾶς ἡμῶν
readings.en: I took a wife from the seed of our family
readings.plain: a woman from the descendants of our own family line

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: ἔλαβον Ἅνναν γυναῖκα ἐκ τοῦ σπέρματος τῆς πατριᾶς ἡμῶν
readings.en: I took Anna as wife from the seed of our family
readings.plain: Anna, a woman from the descendants of our own family line

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus.

a: in the keeping of my kinsman Gabael son of Gabri
t: Gabael "son of" or "brother of" Gabri, and where
p: Sinaiticus: Gabael son of Gabri, in Media. Vaticanus: Gabael, brother of Gabrias, at Rages.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: παρεθέμην Γαβήλῳ βαλλάντια τῷ ἀδελφῷ τῷ Γαβρεὶ
readings.en: I deposited with Gabael, the brother, the (son) of Gabri
readings.plain: in the keeping of my kinsman Gabael son of Gabri

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: παρεθέμην Γαβαήλῳ τῷ ἀδελφῷ Γαβρία ἐν Ῥάγοις τῆς Μηδίας
readings.en: I deposited with Gabael the brother of Gabrias at Rages in Media
readings.plain: in the keeping of Gabael, the brother of Gabrias, at Rages

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus and reads "the brother" as "my kinsman" and "of Gabri" as "son of Gabri," as Sinaiticus itself has in 4:20. Vaticanus's "brother of Gabrias" is followed by the KJV.

a: his son Sennacherib
p: Vaticanus calls the king Acheriel here and in 1:18; Sinaiticus has Sennacherib.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: Σενναχηρεὶμ υἱὸς αὐτοῦ
readings.plain: his son Sennacherib

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: Ἀχηρεὶλ ὁ υἱὸς αὐτοῦ
readings.plain: his son Acheriel

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus, which has the king's real name. "Acheriel" in Vaticanus (again in 1:18) looks like a damaged form of the name; the KJV prints Sennacherib.

a: Less than forty days later
p: Sinaiticus: forty days; Vaticanus: fifty; a corrector wrote fifty in Sinaiticus's margin. The KJV has 55.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἡμέραι τεσσεράκοντα
readings.plain: Less than forty days later

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text; a corrector of Sinaiticus in the margin (ν΄, 50)
readings.orig: ἡμέραι πεντήκοντα
readings.plain: Less than fifty days later

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. The KJV's "five and fifty" comes from other Greek manuscripts. History puts the murder about twenty years after 701 BC (see the note).

a: all your ways into a song of grief
p: Sinaiticus has "ways", Vaticanus "merrymaking"; Amos 8:10 itself has "songs".

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: πᾶσαι αἱ ὁδοὶ ὑμῶν εἰς θρῆνος
readings.plain: all your ways into a song of grief

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: πᾶσαι αἱ εὐφροσύναι ὑμῶν εἰς θρῆνον
readings.plain: all your merrymaking into a song of grief

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus as written. Its "ways" (hodoi) is probably a slip for "songs" (ōdai), the reading of the Hebrew of Amos 8:10; Vaticanus has a freer paraphrase.

a: That same night I washed and went into my courtyard. I lay down to sleep beside the courtyard wall, with my face uncovered because of the heat
p: Sinaiticus says Tobit washed; Vaticanus says he slept "defiled" after the burial.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: αὐτῇ τῇ νυκτὶ ἐλουσάμην καὶ εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὴν αὐλήν μου, καὶ ἐκοιμήθην παρὰ τὸν τοῖχον τῆς αὐλῆς, καὶ τὸ πρόσωπόν μου ἀνακεκαλυμμένον διὰ τὸ καῦμα
readings.en: that night I washed and went into my courtyard and slept by the wall of the courtyard, my face uncovered because of the heat
readings.plain: That same night I washed and went into my courtyard. I lay down to sleep beside the courtyard wall, with my face uncovered because of the heat

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ νυκτὶ ἀνέλυσα θάψας, καὶ ἐκοιμήθην μεμιαμμένος παρὰ τὸν τοῖχον τῆς αὐλῆς, καὶ τὸ πρόσωπόν μου ἀκάλυπτον ἦν
readings.en: that night I came back from burying, and slept defiled by the wall of the courtyard, and my face was uncovered
readings.plain: That same night I came back from the burial and lay down to sleep, unclean, beside the courtyard wall, with my face uncovered

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. In Vaticanus Tobit sleeps outside because he is unclean from touching a corpse (Numbers 19:11) and may not enter the house; in Sinaiticus he has washed and sleeps outside because of the heat.

a: you have not carried the name of even one of them
p: Sinaiticus: "you have not been named after one of them". Vaticanus: "you have had no benefit from one of them".

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἑνὸς αὐτῶν οὐκ ὠνομάσθης
readings.en: you were not named by one of them
readings.plain: you have not carried the name of even one of them

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: ἑνὸς αὐτῶν οὐκ ὠνάσθης
readings.en: you have had no profit of one of them
readings.plain: you have not had the joy of even one of them

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus: she never became any man's wife in name, since no marriage was completed. The two Greek verbs differ by two letters, so one is likely a copying change of the other.

a: the glory of God
t: Before God, or before "the great Raphael"?
p: Vaticanus says the prayers were heard "before the glory of the great Raphael".

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἐνώπιον τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ
readings.plain: the glory of God

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: ἐνώπιον τῆς δόξης τοῦ μεγάλου Ῥαφαήλ
readings.en: before the glory of the great Raphael
readings.plain: the glory of the great Raphael

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. Vaticanus's wording would make the angel the one before whom the prayers are heard; read with 12:12–15, where Raphael brings the prayers before the Lord, it has been taken as support for angels' part in prayer. The KJV, from other manuscripts, has "the majesty of the great God."
b: On whether angels carry prayers to God, see the card at 1 Enoch 99.

a: to set her free from Asmodeus
p: Sinaiticus: Raphael is sent to "loose" Asmodeus from Sarah; Vaticanus: to "bind" Asmodeus.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: λῦσαι Ἀσμοδαῖον
readings.en: to loose Asmodeus the evil demon from her
readings.plain: to set her free from Asmodeus

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: δῆσαι Ἀσμόδαυν
readings.en: to bind Asmodeus the evil demon
readings.plain: to bind Asmodeus

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. Both fit 8:3, where Raphael binds the demon. Jesus uses the same pair of verbs of Satan: one must "bind the strong man" (Mark 3:27), and a woman bound by Satan is "loosed" (Luke 13:16).

a: and so will all who do what is right
p: Sinaiticus stops after "and to all who do what is right"; it is missing from here to the middle of 4:19.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ποιοῦσι τὴν δικαιοσύνην
readings.en: and [success] to all who do what is right
readings.plain: and so will all who do what is right

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete: the text breaks off here
readings.orig: καὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς ποιοῦσιν δικαιοσύνην
readings.en: and to all who do what is right . . .
readings.plain: and to all who do what is right . . .

why: In Sinaiticus the phrase begins a sentence whose end is lost, together with 4:7–19a. The Plain completes it as Vaticanus does. Modern translations that follow Sinaiticus fill the gap from Vaticanus or from the Old Latin version, which scholars use as a witness to the longer text (Fitzmyer).

a: Give alms from what you own, and do not give them with a grudging eye. Never turn your face from someone who is poor; then God will never turn his face from you
p: This verse is missing from Sinaiticus (the gap runs from 4:6 to 4:19). The Plain follows Vaticanus.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων σοι ποίει ἐλεημοσύνην, καὶ μὴ φθονεσάτω σου ὁ ὀφθαλμὸς ἐν τῷ ποιεῖν σε ἐλεημοσύνην· καὶ μὴ ἀποστρέψῃς τὸ πρόσωπόν σου ἀπὸ παντὸς πτωχοῦ, καὶ ἀπὸ σοῦ οὐ μὴ ἀποστραφῇ τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ θεοῦ.
readings.plain: Give alms from what you own, and do not give them with a grudging eye. Never turn your face from someone who is poor; then God will never turn his face from you

a: alms rescue from death
t: The Latin: "from all sin and from death"
p: Jerome's Latin, the Catholic Bible for centuries, says alms free "from all sin and from death" (Vulgate 4:11).

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: ἐλεημοσύνη ἐκ θανάτου ῥύεται
readings.plain: alms rescue from death

readings.w: Latin Vulgate of Jerome (Clementine edition, 1592), Tobit 4:11; Douay-Rheims "alms deliver from all sin, and from death"
readings.orig: eleemosyna ab omni peccato et a morte liberat
readings.en: alms frees from all sin and from death
readings.plain: alms set free from all sin and from death

why: The Plain translates the Greek. Jerome made his Tobit from an Aramaic copy and his own paraphrase, and his "from all sin" brings in the wording of 12:9. Because Catholic teaching and controversy long used the Latin, this is the form debated at the Reformation (see the card on this page).

Do not marry an outsider, a woman who is not of your father's tribe, because we are the sons of the prophets. Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were our forefathers from the beginning. Remember, son, that all of them married women from among their own kin. They were blessed in their children, and their descendants will inherit the land

readings.orig: (lost)

why: The Plain follows one witness at a time in this verse: Vaticanus through "the Lord himself gives all good things", then Sinaiticus from "Whomever the Lord wishes" to the end. It does not join half a sentence from each. Vaticanus's "every nation does not have counsel" is a Hebrew-style way of saying "no nation has counsel" (see the note).

a: but the Lord himself gives all good things
p: Vaticanus: the Lord himself gives all good things. Where Sinaiticus resumes, it reads: the Lord will give them good counsel.

readings.orig: δώσει Κύριος αὐτοῖς βουλὴν ἀγαθήν
readings.en: the Lord will give them good counsel
readings.plain: the Lord will give them good counsel

why: The Plain stays with Vaticanus to the end of its sentence. Sinaiticus starts again in the middle of a sentence whose beginning is lost, so its "them" has nothing in the surviving text to refer to; the nearest earlier words in Sinaiticus are the end of 4:6, "all who do what is right". Joining Sinaiticus's clause to Vaticanus's "no nation has counsel" would make "them" mean the nations, a sentence found in no manuscript.

p: Sinaiticus: the Lord brings low whomever he wishes, "down to the lowest Hades". Vaticanus ends instead with the obscure "as they wish".

why: From "Whomever the Lord wishes" the Plain follows Sinaiticus, the base text. Its wording echoes Hannah's song, where the LORD brings down to Sheol (1 Samuel 2:6–7). Vaticanus's "as they wish" (plural) is hard to make sense of after "he humbles", which may point to a damaged text.

p: Sinaiticus says Gabael lives in Ecbatana, though 4:1 and 4:20 put him at Rages. The Plain reads Rages.

readings.w: Required by the story (4:1; 4:20; 9:2), and read by the Latin Vulgate of Jerome (5:8); an emendation of the Greek
readings.orig: (emendation) — Vulgate 5:8: qui moratur in Rages civitate Medorum

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: παρὰ Γαβαὴλ τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἡμῶν ηὐλίσθην
readings.en: and I have lodged with Gabael our brother
readings.plain: (names no town)

why: This is an emendation. Sinaiticus as written contradicts itself: in the next breath it measures the road from Ecbatana to Gabael's town, and the rest of the book puts Gabael at Rages. A copyist probably wrote the wrong city, so the Plain corrects it and shows the written reading here. Jerome's Latin, made from a Semitic copy and independent of Sinaiticus, also puts Gabael in Rages. Vaticanus has a shorter speech that names no town.

a: From Ecbatana to Rages is a journey of two regular days, for Rages lies in the hill country and Ecbatana in the middle of the plain
t: "Garrai" and a clause in the margin
p: Sinaiticus reads "to Garrai", a garbled Rages. The first scribe of Sinaiticus seems to have skipped part of this sentence, and the original corrector supplied it in the margin.

readings.en: it is a road of two set days from Ecbatana to Garrai; for they lie in the mountain, Ecbatana in the middle of the plain
readings.plain: From Ecbatana to Garrai is a journey of two regular days, for they lie in the hill country and Ecbatana in the middle of the plain

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: (lacks the clause)

why: The Plain reads Rages for "Garrai," which has not been convincingly identified with a real place; the context requires Gabael's town. Swete's notes say the first scribe of Sinaiticus seems to have left out the words from "to Garrai" to the second "Ecbatana". The scribe's eye probably jumped from one "Ecbatana" to the next, a common slip between like words, and the original corrector (ℵ¹, working with the scribes) supplied the words in the margin. So the margin most likely restores the original text rather than adding to it. On the mistaken geography, see the note.

a: tried to gulp down the boy's foot
t: The boy's foot, or the boy?
p: Sinaiticus: the fish tried to swallow his foot. Vaticanus and the Vulgate: it tried to devour the boy.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἐβούλετο καταπεῖν τὸν πόδα τοῦ παιδαρίου
readings.en: wanted to swallow the boy's foot
readings.plain: tried to gulp down the boy's foot

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text; similarly the Vulgate (6:2)
readings.orig: ἐβουλήθη καταπεῖν τὸ παιδάριον
readings.plain: tried to gulp down the boy

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. Both Greek texts have "a big fish" (the Vulgate: "a huge fish"); they differ only on whether it went for the boy's foot or for the boy himself. Sinaiticus's foot fits a boy standing in the river washing his feet. A later corrector of Sinaiticus added "from fear" before "he shouted."

a: coming near Ecbatana
p: Sinaiticus: they came near Ecbatana. Vaticanus and the KJV: "near to Rages".

readings.orig: ἤγγιζεν εἰς Ἐκβάτανα
readings.en: he was already drawing near to Ecbatana
readings.plain: coming near Ecbatana

readings.orig: προσήγγισαν τῇ Ῥάγῃ
readings.plain: coming near Rages

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. Raguel lives in Ecbatana (3:7, in both texts), so Vaticanus's Rages here is a slip, though the KJV follows it.

a: When we come back from Rages, we will hold her wedding
p: Sinaiticus first says "when we come back from Raguel", then later in the verse "from Rages". The Plain reads Rages both times.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text (Sinaiticus has the same words, with ἐπιστρέψωμεν, in the second half of the verse: ὅταν ἐπιστρέψωμεν ἐκ Ῥάγων)
readings.orig: ὅταν ὑποστρέψωμεν ἐκ Ῥάγων
readings.plain: When we come back from Rages, we will hold her wedding

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete, first half of the verse
readings.orig: ὅταν ἐπιστρέψωμεν ἐκ Ῥαγουὴλ
readings.plain: When we come back from Raguel's, we will hold her wedding

why: Raphael's plan is to fetch the money at Rages and marry on the way home, so "from Raguel" makes no sense; a copyist confused the two similar names. Sinaiticus says the same thing twice in this verse; one possible explanation, offered here as a guess, is that two forms of the sentence were joined. Note that the story then goes another way: the wedding takes place at Raguel's house at once (7:9–14), and Raphael goes on to Rages alone to fetch the money (9:1–5).

a: When you are about to lie with her, the two of you must first get up and pray
p: In Jerome's Latin, Raphael tells Tobias to keep apart from Sarah and pray with her for three nights.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ὅταν μέλλῃς γίνεσθαι μετ᾽ αὐτῆς, ἐξεγέρθητε πρῶτον ἀμφότεροι καὶ προσεύξασθε καὶ δεήθητε τοῦ κυρίου τοῦ οὐρανοῦ
readings.en: when you are about to be with her, both of you first rise and pray and beg the Lord of heaven
readings.plain: When you are about to lie with her, the two of you must first get up and pray

readings.w: Latin Vulgate of Jerome (Clementine edition), Tobit 6:18 (the longer passage is 6:16–22); Douay-Rheims
readings.orig: per tres dies continens esto ab ea, et nihil aliud nisi orationibus vacabis cum ea
readings.en: for three days you will keep yourself from her, and give yourself to nothing else but prayers with her
readings.plain: For three days keep yourself from her, and give yourself to nothing but prayer with her

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Vulgate's longer speech (6:16–22) is not in any Greek manuscript and probably comes from Jerome's free translation of his Aramaic copy. It shaped Catholic reading of Tobit for over a thousand years (see the note on this verse).
